atoms.text:
In the U.S., elections are held for government officials at the federal, state, and local levels. At the federal level, the president is elected indirectly every four years by the people of each state through an Electoral College.
Presidential candidates need to be at least 35 years old, be born in the USA and pay for their political campaigns themselves.

atoms.text:
Prior to Election Day
In each state, all parties with a presidential candidate choose potential electors. Who is chosen to be an elector, how, and when varies by state. Based on its representation in Congress, each state has a certain number of electors.

All states have the same amount of electors.

atoms.text:
Election Day
Election Day is always on the Tuesday following the first Monday in November. The people in each state cast their votes for their state's electors. The party with more votes in a particular state wins all electors of that state. The opposing party's votes are lost.
Citizens can vote directly at their respective polling station. Some states offer vote-by-mail programs that allow registered citizens to vote in advance.

After Election Day
The electors meet to vote for the president and their votes are counted by Congress. The newly elected president is inaugurated in January.

atoms.text:
In the US, First-Past-The-Post voting is applied. This is a single-winner voting rule which in the case of federal election results in the rule that the party with more initial votes wins all electoral candidates of one state and the opposing parties' votes are lost.

Due to this, it is possible that a candidate wins the election although they did not win the popular vote. This already happened several times in the history of US-American federal elections.

atoms.text: The question whether it is fair that the Electoral College can differ from the popular vote comes up repeatedly in U.S. politics. After several elections where the winner of the popular vote did not become president, public debate has intensified. There are ongoing discussions about whether the system should be changed or whether it still serves an important purpose.

atoms.text: Midterm elections are held every four years in the middle of a U.S. President’s term, when voters elect all members of the House of Representatives and about one-third of the Senate. They are important because they determine which party controls Congress, shaping the president’s ability to pass laws. If the opposing party wins control, it can block the president’s agenda and increase the risk of political standoffs, sometimes even leading to a government shutdown over budget disputes. If the president’s party loses significant power, the president may be seen as a “lame duck,” with reduced influence for the rest of the term.
